title: E-Commerce Platforms, Not Delivery Riders, Must Now Pay GST on Local Delivery From 1 November
meta_description: From 1 November 2026, e-commerce operators must pay 5% GST without input credit on delivery services booked through their apps, CBIC notifications show.
court: Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs
case_name: Notification No. 09/2026-Central Tax (Rate) read with Notification No. 06/2026-Central Tax (Rate)
citation: Notification No. 09/2026-Central Tax (Rate) dated 27 October 2026, amending Notification No. 17/2017-Central Tax (Rate) issued under Section 9(5) of the CGST Act, 2017, read with Notification No. 06/2026-Central Tax (Rate) prescribing the applicable rate; both effective from 1 November 2026
body: Anyone who has ordered food, groceries or a parcel through an app and watched the delivery fee appear as a separate line item has, until now, been looking at a service that attracted GST at 18 per cent, with the tax position often unclear as to who was actually meant to deposit it. Two notifications issued by the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs on 27 October 2026, effective from 1 November 2026, bring that uncertainty to an end, and shift the compliance burden squarely onto the platforms rather than the individual delivery workers or small operators who physically carry out the delivery.

Notification No. 09/2026-Central Tax (Rate) amends the existing Notification No. 17/2017-Central Tax (Rate), the notification issued under Section 9(5) of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 that lists services on which an e-commerce operator, rather than the actual supplier, must pay GST. The amendment broadens the relevant entry from the narrower category of 'local delivery' services to the wider category of 'delivery services' generally, carving out postal and courier services, which continue to be taxed under the ordinary rules rather than this special regime.

Whether the new rule applies to a given delivery turns on whether the person actually carrying it out, typically an individual rider or a small delivery partner, is liable to be registered under Section 22(1) of the CGST Act on account of their turnover. Where that delivery provider falls below the registration threshold and would not otherwise be paying GST on the service, the e-commerce operator through whose platform the delivery was booked now steps into the shoes of the supplier for GST purposes and must account for the tax itself, under the Section 9(5) mechanism the amendment extends to this wider category of services.

The rate at which that tax is to be paid comes from a companion notification, Notification No. 06/2026-Central Tax (Rate), which fixes it at 5 per cent without the benefit of input tax credit. Matching notifications under the Integrated Goods and Services Tax Act and the Union Territory Goods and Services Tax Act were issued the same day, so the changes apply uniformly whether the delivery crosses state lines or stays within one union territory.

For the riders and small delivery operators who actually do the work, the change is largely one of relief from a compliance burden they were poorly placed to carry in the first place. Riders working below the registration threshold were never meant to be filing GST returns on their delivery fees, and shifting the liability to the platform that aggregates thousands of such deliveries puts the paperwork where the resources to handle it actually sit, rather than on an individual earning a delivery fee of a few rupees at a time.

Platforms themselves face the heavier compliance lift. The many food-delivery, quick-commerce and logistics-aggregator businesses that run on venture capital and, in several cases, foreign institutional money, the change means recalibrating pricing, invoicing and tax-reporting systems ahead of every delivery fee charged on or after 1 November 2026. A platform that continues to treat delivery fees as outside its own GST liability, on the assumption that the delivery partner bears that burden, risks a demand for the 5 per cent tax it should have collected and deposited itself, along with the interest and penalty that typically follow a Section 9(5) default once a tax authority notices the gap.

Postal and courier services sit outside this new entry altogether and continue to be taxed under the ordinary, pre-amendment rules, so platforms that route certain deliveries through a registered courier rather than an individual rider need to keep that distinction clear in their systems rather than applying the new 5 per cent, no-credit treatment across every delivery booked through the app without checking which category it actually falls into.

The change lands at a moment when e-commerce platforms, many of them structured with foreign investment and some run by or for foreign parent companies entering the Indian market through a local subsidiary, are already working through a run of GST changes that took effect on the same date, including new rules on post-sale discounts, credit notes and e-commerce seller registration. Getting the delivery-services treatment right from day one matters because the liability sits with the platform, not with the rider, and a tax authority auditing a platform's returns will be looking at exactly this entry when it checks compliance with Section 9(5).
why_it_matters: E-commerce and quick-commerce platforms, including foreign-backed and foreign-owned operators running Indian subsidiaries, now carry direct GST liability on delivery fees charged through their apps, rather than being able to treat that liability as the delivery rider's problem. Getting this wrong exposes the platform itself to a tax demand with interest and penalty, so any foreign company entering or already operating in India's e-commerce or delivery space needs its billing and GST-reporting systems updated to reflect the 5 per cent, no-input-credit treatment from 1 November 2026 onward.
card_summary: From 1 November 2026, CBIC notifications make e-commerce operators, not delivery riders, liable for 5% GST without input tax credit on delivery services booked through their apps, under an expanded Section 9(5) entry.
card_tip: Check whether your platform's billing system now treats delivery fees as the platform's own 5% GST liability under Section 9(5), rather than assuming the rider or courier bears it.
verification_notes: AUDIENCE: foreign company (e-commerce, quick-commerce and logistics platforms operating in India through a local subsidiary, including foreign-backed operators). TARGET QUERY: who pays GST on delivery charges on e-commerce platforms from November 2026. DEMAND EVIDENCE: none seen (no search-volume data available; selected because it is a dated, numbered regulatory change with immediate practical impact on e-commerce operators, a sector the firm's foreign-company audience frequently asks about). The substance of Notification No. 09/2026-Central Tax (Rate), amending Notification No. 17/2017-Central Tax (Rate) under Section 9(5) of the CGST Act to widen the 'local delivery' entry to 'delivery services' generally while excluding postal and courier services, and its effective date of 1 November 2026, are corroborated across the CalcGuru, The Tax Corp, Taxo.online and A2Z Taxcorp reports found in this run, which in turn describe the notification text consistently with each other. The 5 per cent, no-input-tax-credit rate from the companion Notification No. 06/2026-Central Tax (Rate), and the issuance of matching IGST and UTGST notifications the same day, are also corroborated across more than one of these sources. The notifications themselves are dated 27 October 2026, a few days before the scope window for this run begins on 1 November 2026; they are reported here by their effective, operative date of 1 November 2026, the date on which the changed GST treatment actually took hold and became practically relevant, rather than by their earlier gazette date, and that distinction is flagged here rather than left unstated. This is a regulator notification, not a court ruling, reported under the news.md scope's provision for regulator circulars with a specific number and date and a practical impact. The official CBIC gazette text was not accessed in this session; the description above rests on the secondary commentary cited, which was consistent across all sources opened.
